Journal (General Ledger)

journal_entries and journal_lines are Merlin's authoritative double-entry ledger. Every figure on the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Trial Balance, and an individual account's transaction view is a sum over these two tables — not a re-derivation from invoice headers computed at report time. JournalService (app/Modules/Accounting/Services/) is the only class permitted to write to them.

Why a journal

Before the journal existed, each report independently re-derived debits and credits from documents/document_lines, with its own copy of the status filters that decide what counts. That duplication drifted: one report's revenue query excluded a status the application never actually writes, so a voided sales invoice's revenue kept showing up there while correctly disappearing from the others. A single authoritative posting, written once at the moment a document's ledger effect becomes real, removes the class of bug rather than the one instance of it.

Shape of an entry

TableKey columns
journal_entriesdocument_id (nullable), entry_date, source, description, reversed_by_id
journal_linesjournal_entry_id, account_id, party_id (nullable), debit, credit, description

An entry always has two or more lines, and the sum of every line's debit must equal the sum of every line's credit — JournalService::post() rejects (UnbalancedJournalEntryException) anything that doesn't. source identifies what kind of event produced the entry (sales_invoice_issued, purchase_invoice_posted, payment, credit_note_applied); together with document_id it makes posting idempotent — calling post() a second time for the same document and source is a no-op that returns the existing entry rather than creating a duplicate.

Append-only

Nothing ever calls update() or delete() on a JournalEntry or JournalLine. To unwind a posting — an invoice gets voided, for example — JournalService::reverse() writes a new entry with every line's debit and credit swapped, and stamps reversed_by_id on the original. The original stays exactly as it was posted.

Swap, not negate A reversal swaps debit and credit on each line rather than negating one side. A report computing a signed total for an account must therefore sum credit − debit (or the reverse for a debit-normal account) — summing only one side leaves a reversal with no visible effect, since the reversing line lands entirely on the other column.

Posted documents are immutable

Once a document has a non-reversed JournalEntry, its DocumentLine rows refuse to be saved or deleted — DocumentLine::saving()/deleting() throw PostedDocumentImmutableException. This is what makes the ledger's append-only guarantee real rather than aspirational: without it, editing a posted invoice's line would silently leave the already-posted entry wrong, with nothing to notice.

The guard is bypassed by saveQuietly(), used by two trusted system paths that legitimately rewrite a posted invoice's line amounts after the fact: foreign-exchange rate finalisation in DocumentService::recordPayment(), and the VAT correction applied when a payment notification confirms a foreign-currency invoice's true local amount (PaymentNotificationMatcher::applyCorrectedAmount()). Both are already restricted to invoices confirmed not yet posted at the point they run.

What posts, and when

DocumentService posts at every event that changes what's owed:

EventMethodEntry
Sales invoice sentmarkAsSent()Debit accounts receivable for the invoice total; credit each line's income account; credit the VAT liability account for any tax
Sales invoice voidedvoidDocument()Reverses the issuing entry, if one exists
Purchase invoice postedpost() / postAutonomously()Debit each line's expense account; credit accounts payable for the invoice total
Payment received or madecreatePaymentDocument() (bank-statement settlement), recordPurchasePayment(), and BillingService::recordPayment() — all via the shared postPaymentJournal()Debit/credit the bank (contra) account against the receivable or payable account
Credit note appliedapplyCreditNote()Debit each of the credit note's own income accounts (reversing the recognised revenue); credit the target invoice's receivable account

When posting is skipped vs. when it fails

Posting is silently skipped — not an error — when a document's receivable or payable account, or a line's income or expense account, isn't configured yet. This mirrors a guard the old report queries already relied on (they excluded rows with a null account id), just moved from report time to write time: an invoice with an unallocated line was never counted before, and still isn't.

The one case that fails loudly instead: a sales invoice carrying VAT (tax_total > 0) with no VAT liability account configured in Settings › Billing. That's a real configuration gap on a business that has told Merlin it's VAT-registered, not an in-progress document waiting on account allocation — markAsSent() throws rather than posting an entry that would silently misstate VAT.

Which reports read the journal

Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Trial Balance, and an individual account's transaction view read journal_lines directly — each collapses to a single grouped query.

Income by Account, Income by Client, Expenses by Account, and Expenses by Supplier deliberately still read documents/document_lines directly. Each needs data the journal doesn't preserve at that granularity — an invoice count, the outstanding balance_due, or VAT split out per line rather than summed once per account across a whole invoice — and neither has the reversal-drift risk the journal exists to fix: sales-side status filtering already excludes voided invoices by status directly, and purchase invoices only ever move forward through posted → partially_paid → paid, with no reversal case to get wrong.

The balance_due formula

A related but separate concern: Document::recalculateBalance() is the single formula (total − amount_paid − credits_applied, floored at zero) that every writer of a document's balance_due must go through. applyCreditNote(), recordPayment(), and Document::recalculateTotals() all call it rather than assigning balance_due directly. credits_applied stores a credit note's amount uncapped — the same floor-at-zero in the formula handles a credit note larger than what remained owed, so nothing needs to clamp the credit itself.

A note on Eloquent date columns

A model attribute cast to 'date' is still stored as a full Y-m-d H:i:s value — Eloquent's fromDateTime() formats every date-typed cast using the connection's datetime format regardless of cast type. journal_entries.entry_date is affected the same as every other date column in this app, so any query filtering on it uses whereDate(), never a raw where() comparison — the latter silently fails to match because of the stored value's trailing time component.
